description: Frozen RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) test vectors. ATL hashes entry metadata as SHA256(JCS(metadata)), so every byte of JCS output is protocol-visible: two implementations that canonicalize differently produce different metadata_hash values and therefore different leaf hashes and different roots.

origins.rfc8785-published: Verbatim from RFC 8785. The Section 3.2.2 / 3.2.3 worked example and its canonical output are additionally byte-checked against the hexadecimal dump the RFC prints in Section 3.2.4. The Appendix B rows are the RFC's own Table 1.
origins.rfc8785-derived: No published example covers this input; the expected output was written by reading the rule text in the cited section. Integer-only, so the ES6 floating-point algorithm of Section 3.2.2.3 is not involved and the expected value is decidable by inspection.
origins.rfc8785-input-constraint: No published example covers this input either. RFC 8785 Section 3.1 states three MUST requirements on the data to be canonicalized, and Section 3.2.2.3 a fourth on NaN/Infinity; these cases record, for each, an input that breaks it and the fact that a conformant implementation must not return a canonical form for it. The expected OUTCOME is read off the rule text; where a case instead expects success, the `expected` string is the ECMA-262 Section 7.1.12.1 rendering the RFC mandates, decidable without running atl-core.

provenance.not_generated_by_atl_core: No expected value in this file was produced by running atl-core. The `conformance` field describes atl-core's current behaviour; the `expected` field never does.

conformance_legend.pass: atl-core produces the RFC-mandated output for this input.
conformance_legend.known_divergence: atl-core does NOT produce the RFC-mandated output for this input. The RFC value is recorded unchanged in `expected`; it was deliberately not adjusted to match atl-core. `atl_core_actual` pins what atl-core emits instead. The test suite asserts BOTH that the output still differs from `expected` and that it still equals `atl_core_actual`, so the case fails on a repair (remove the marker) and equally on a new, different bug -- an assertion of mere inequality would have accepted any wrong answer at all.
conformance_legend.atl_core_actual: atl_core_actual is a REGRESSION PIN, not an expected value: it records the wrong output atl-core produces today, so that the test can tell a repair (output becomes the RFC value) apart from a fresh breakage (output becomes something else again). It is the one field in these vector files that is deliberately taken from the implementation, and it is only ever attached to a case already marked known_divergence. `expected` is never touched by it.
conformance_legend.empty_known_divergences: `known_divergences` is currently empty, and every case below is marked `pass`: atl-core meets every RFC value in this file. The marker vocabulary is kept documented rather than deleted, because a future divergence must be recorded this way -- with the RFC value left untouched -- and not by editing `expected`.
conformance_legend.input_constraint_cases: Cases in `input_constraint_cases` pin the RFC 8785 Section 3.1 constraints on canonicalization INPUT rather than an output string. `expects` is `error` when the input must be refused, `canonical` when it has a canonical form -- including where that output NORMALISES the spelling the author wrote, which is what canonicalization is for -- or `not_confirmable` when the input cannot be judged at all and the implementation must decline to confirm it rather than accept or reject it. `checked_by` names the layer that acts: `check_unique_property_names` reads the raw text before a parser can collapse duplicates; `receipt_deserialize` means the whole receipt must be refused by plain `serde_json::from_str::<Receipt>` and `from_reader`, the paths that go around every constructor; `receipt_provenance` means no inspection is possible at all and the receipt must instead be ineligible for confirmation; `canonicalize` sees a parsed value; and `json_parser` means the constraint is enforced by serde_json at parse time and this crate only pins that it is.

canonicalization_cases.name: rfc8785_3_2_2_worked_example
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Sections 3.2.2 (input) and 3.2.3 (output); output byte-checked against the Section 3.2.4 hexadecimal dump
canonicalization_cases.note: Exercises both halves of number handling at once: the literal 333333333.33333329 must PARSE to 0x41b3de4355555555, and 1E30 / 1e-27 must RENDER in exponential form with a signed exponent. Key ordering, literals and string escaping are exercised in the same case.

canonicalization_cases.name: rfc8785_3_2_3_property_sorting
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3, "The following JSON test data can be used for verifying the correctness of the sorting scheme"; the RFC publishes the expected property order, and `expected` is that published order written out with Section 3.2.2.2 escaping
canonicalization_cases.input_json_text:
{
  "\u20ac": "Euro Sign",
  "\r": "Carriage Return",
  "\ufb33": "Hebrew Letter Dalet With Dagesh",
  "1": "One",
  "\ud83d\ude00": "Emoji: Grinning Face",
  "\u0080": "Control",
  "\u00f6": "Latin Small Letter O With Diaeresis"
}
canonicalization_cases.expected: {"\r":"Carriage Return","1":"One","":"Control","ö":"Latin Small Letter O With Diaeresis","€":"Euro Sign","😀":"Emoji: Grinning Face","דּ":"Hebrew Letter Dalet With Dagesh"}
canonicalization_cases.note: Sorting is by UTF-16 code units, so U+FB33 sorts after U+1F600 even though U+1F600 has the larger code point: its UTF-16 form starts with the surrogate U+D83D, which is below U+FB33.

canonicalization_cases.name: unicode_keys
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3 UTF-16 code unit order

canonicalization_cases.name: array_order_preserved
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3: array element order MUST NOT change, but objects inside are sorted

canonicalization_cases.name: unicode_not_escaped
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2: values outside U+0000-U+001F are emitted as is

canonicalization_cases.name: control_characters
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2: U+0000-U+001F use lowercase \uhhhh unless one of \b \t \n \f \r

canonicalization_cases.name: named_control_escapes
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2: U+0008, U+0009, U+000A, U+000C, U+000D use the named escapes

canonicalization_cases.name: empty_key_sorts_first
canonicalization_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3: the shorter string precedes the longer when it is a prefix

number_serialization_cases.comment: First value at the ECMA-262 exponential threshold: decimal exponent 21
Negative side of the threshold: decimal exponent -7, so exponential form; the next row up stays positional
Round to even. Appendix B note (4): the value is exactly 1424953923781206.25, equidistant between two shortest representations, and the ECMA-262 Note 2 rule takes the even digit

input_constraint_cases.name: duplicate_property_name_root
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names
input_constraint_cases.note: Not detectable after parsing: serde_json keeps the last occurrence, so the value is indistinguishable from {"x":2} and would canonicalize happily. RFC 8259 Section 4 makes the choice of survivor unpredictable across parsers, so two verifiers can hash two different objects out of these same bytes.

input_constraint_cases.name: duplicate_property_name_nested
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names
input_constraint_cases.note: The refusal must name the RFC 6901 JSON Pointer of the offending object; on nested metadata a refusal without a location is not actionable. `error_path` is the pointer, not a value from the RFC.

input_constraint_cases.name: duplicate_property_name_lost_on_every_serde_path
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Section 3.1, and the limits of any API that does not see the bytes
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names
input_constraint_cases.note: A whole receipt carrying a duplicate deep in entry.metadata, routed around Receipt::from_json -- through serde_json::from_str::<Receipt> and through serde_json::from_value. Receipt derives Deserialize publicly, so both are reachable by any consumer and no constructor can intercept them. Neither is a DETECTION case and neither may be written as one: serde_json keeps the last occurrence, and from_value is additionally handed a Value that an earlier parse already flattened, so by then there is nothing left to detect. The RFC 8785 Section 3.1 constraint is a property of a BYTE STREAM, and no API accepting a parsed structure can check it. An earlier revision of atl-core replaced serde_json's Deserialize impl for the metadata field with a hand-written visitor that refused duplicates during deserialization; it was withdrawn because under serde_json/arbitrary_precision -- which any crate in a consumer's dependency graph can enable, and Cargo unifies onto every crate in it -- deserialize_any delivers a non-integer number as a map keyed by the private token $serde_json::private::Number, so such a visitor builds an object where a number belongs: every metadata hash changes, and a document containing that literal object collides with one containing the number. What the case pins instead is provenance: a Receipt records whether its own bytes were ever checked, no serde path can set that record, the marker cannot be assigned across from a receipt that was checked, and ReceiptVerifier::verify declines to confirm a receipt that lacks it. The verdict is `not evaluated`, never `invalid` -- nothing about this receipt was disproved.
input_constraint_cases.metadata_hash_derivation: metadata_hash is SHA-256 of {"claims":[{"v":1},{"v":2}]}, the JCS form of what this document's metadata FLATTENS to once the duplicate is lost. Computed independently (hashlib over that exact string), not by running atl-core, and canonical by inspection: the keys are already sorted and there is no whitespace. It is set correctly on purpose -- with a placeholder hash the verifier stops at step 1 and the case would pass without ever reaching the provenance gate it exists to test.

input_constraint_cases.name: duplicate_property_name_distinct_values_only
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names
input_constraint_cases.note: The accepting side of the same boundary: the same name in DIFFERENT objects is not a duplicate. Without this case a checker that refused every repeated string anywhere would pass the two cases above.

input_constraint_cases.name: number_beyond_double_precision_is_normalised
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^53 + 1, the smallest positive integer no double holds. It denotes the double 2^53 and MUST serialize as that double's ECMA-262 Section 7.1.12.1 spelling. Refusing it -- which this crate did in a pre-release draft -- reads Section 3.1's MUST as an instruction to the serializer; Appendix B note (1) says the opposite in as many words: "how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm".

input_constraint_cases.name: appendix_b_2_pow_68_integer_text_is_normalised
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^68 written out exactly. RFC 8785 Appendix B Table 1 requires the double 0x4430000000000000 -- which is precisely this integer -- to serialize as 295147905179352830000, and note (2) says the algorithm does not take its "extended precision" into consideration. The RFC normalizes a large integer by its own published table; it does not reject one. The same double is frozen from the other direction in number_serialization_cases, row 4430000000000000.

input_constraint_cases.name: appendix_b_max_safe_integer_boundary
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^53, Appendix B Table 1 row 4340000000000000 ("Max pos int"), reached as integer TEXT rather than as a double. Fixes the boundary from the accepting side: the value one above it normalizes to this one.

input_constraint_cases.name: unsigned_integer_beyond_double_precision_is_normalised
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^64 - 1, which only fits u64. Kept because the obvious representability check written in u64 SUCCEEDS here -- (u64::MAX as f64) as u64 saturates back to u64::MAX -- so an implementation that refuses on representability must not be lulled by it. Under the correct rule no such check exists at all.

input_constraint_cases.name: ordinary_large_integer_is_normalised
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: An ordinary 19-digit integer, not a power of two: the shape a nanosecond timestamp or a fixed-point amount takes in real metadata. It denotes the double 1756812345678901248 and serializes as that double's shortest spelling.

input_constraint_cases.name: exact_double_written_non_canonically_2_pow_62
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^62 is exactly representable, and is still normalized: what decides the output is the double, never the digits. A draft rule refused this, which meant reporting `untrusted` for a receipt a JavaScript verifier reports valid -- a claimed inability where the ability plainly exists.

input_constraint_cases.name: exact_double_written_non_canonically_2_pow_60
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: 2^60, the same shape at a magnitude ordinary metadata reaches -- a byte count or a bit mask lands here without anything exotic. One case could be dismissed as a corner; two at different magnitudes fix the rule.

input_constraint_cases.name: normalised_spelling_is_a_fixed_point
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: The output of the 2^62 case fed back in. It is NOT itself an exact double (it lies between 2^62 and the next double up), so a rule demanding exact representability would refuse the canonicalizer's own output and canonicalization would not be a fixed point. Every case in this group must survive being re-fed to the canonicalizer unchanged, and the test asserts that for all of them.

input_constraint_cases.name: safe_integers_are_emitted_verbatim
input_constraint_cases.source: RFC 8785 Appendix B notes (1) and (2), and Section 3.2.2.3
input_constraint_cases.constraint: none on the serializer: Section 3.1's number MUST binds the producer of the data, and Appendix B note (1) states that how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm
input_constraint_cases.note: The whole ECMA-262 safe-integer range, which is all ordinary metadata, is emitted digit for digit. Normalization changes nothing here, so the output is byte-identical to what a naive implementation produces -- which is why this repair does not disturb receipts that hold only ordinary integers.

input_constraint_cases.name: lone_surrogate_escape
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON string data MUST be expressible as Unicode
input_constraint_cases.note: An unpaired high surrogate is not a Unicode scalar value and has no UTF-8 encoding. serde_json refuses it at parse time, so it can never reach canonicalization; the case exists to make that guarantee observable rather than assumed, since it is enforced by a dependency and not by this crate's code.

input_constraint_cases.name: lone_surrogate_escape_low
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON string data MUST be expressible as Unicode

input_constraint_cases.name: well_formed_surrogate_pair
input_constraint_cases.constraint: JSON string data MUST be expressible as Unicode
input_constraint_cases.note: The accepting side: a well-formed surrogate PAIR is one scalar value, U+1F600, and Section 3.2.2.2 emits it as UTF-8 rather than escaped. Without this case a parser that refused every \ud8xx escape would pass the two above.
